meaning: A soft, polite request in the form “I would be grateful if you could ...”.
connection: Verb te-form + いただけると (いただければ) ありがたい／幸いです

senses.label: Soft request
senses.meaning: On the surface it expresses gratitude, but it is really a request. It is much softer than 「〜てください」. It leaves the decision to the listener and puts no pressure on them.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + いただけるとありがたいです (ありがたいのですが)
examples: I would appreciate it if you could reply by tomorrow.
I'd be grateful if you could be a little quieter.

senses.label: Formal written style
senses.meaning: Business emails often use 「幸いです」 or 「助かります」 instead. 「〜いただけますと幸いです」 and 「〜いただければ幸いです」 are the most formal.
senses.connection: te-form / お・ご + verb stem or Sino-Japanese noun + いただけますと (いただければ) 幸いです
examples: I would be grateful if you could consider this.
It would really help if you could send me the documents.
I would appreciate it if you could get in touch.

senses.label: Casual version
senses.meaning: With friends or peers, use 「〜てもらえるとありがたい」 or 「〜てもらえると助かる」. It sounds relaxed but is still more polite than a direct command.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + もらえると (もらえたら) ありがたい／助かる
examples: It'd be great if you could give me a hand.
It'd really help if you could drive me to the station.

notes: Use it only for something the other person has not done yet. If they have already done it, switch to thanking: ✕ (after receiving the reply) 「ご返信いただけるとありがたいです」 → ○ 「ご返信いただき、ありがとうございます」.
Do not use 「〜てもらえるとありがたい」 or 「〜てもらえると助かる」 with superiors or clients. 「もらう」 is not respectful enough and sounds casual; use 「いただける」.
After 「お／ご + verb」, attach 「いただける」 directly without inserting 「して」: ✕ 「ご確認していただけると」 → ○ 「ご確認いただけると」.

The tone is “it would be great if you could ...”, which sounds optional. If you use it for a deadline or a rule that must be followed, the other person may think it is not mandatory; in that case use 「〜ようお願いいたします」 or 「必ず〜てください」.

daily.title: Asking a neighbor to be quieter
daily.description: The neighbor is noisy at night, and you ask politely.
daily.example: I'd appreciate it if you could keep the volume down a bit at night.

daily.title: Asking a friend for help
daily.description: You ask a friend to help you move.
daily.example: It'd really help if you could help me move on Saturday.

work.title: Business email asking for a check
work.description: You sent documents to a client and ask them to review them.
work.example: I would be grateful if you could review the attached documents.

work.title: Asking your boss for time
work.description: You want to talk something over with your manager.
work.example: I'd appreciate it if you could spare me a few minutes.

etymology: 「いただける」 is the potential form of 「いただく」 (to humbly receive). 「ありがたい」 originally meant “hard to come by, rare”, and later “worthy of thanks”. Literally the phrase says “if I could receive this from you, it would be a rare blessing”, which became a fixed soft request.

similar.title: 〜ていただけませんか
similar.explanation: 「〜ていただけませんか」 asks the listener a direct question, and they have to answer yes or no. 「〜ていただけるとありがたい」 only states your gratitude without asking, so it puts less pressure on them and suits written requests and requests to clients better.

similar.title: 〜ばと思う（〜ていただければと思います）
similar.explanation: 「〜ていただければと思います」 stops at “that is what I am hoping”, so it is about as soft, and is common in speeches and emails. 「〜ありがたい／幸いです」 says outright “I would be grateful”, so the sentence ends in a more complete way.

similar.title: 〜お〜いただく・ご〜いただく
similar.explanation: Both are built on 「いただく」. 「ご確認いただく」 is itself a humble expression; add 「〜ると幸いです」 and it becomes the most formal form of this pattern, 「ご確認いただけますと幸いです」.

similar.title: 〜てほしい・〜てもらいたい
similar.explanation: 「〜てほしい」 states your own wish directly. Saying 「〜てほしいです」 to a superior or client sounds self-centered and rude. When asking someone above you, use 「〜ていただけるとありがたい」.

formation: It is made of four parts: the te-form of a verb, 「いただける」, 「と」, and 「ありがたい」. 「いただける」 is the potential form of the humble verb 「いただく」 (to receive), meaning “to be able to receive the favor of the other person doing something for me”: the other person is the doer and the speaker is the beneficiary. 「と」 is a hypothetical condition (“if ...”), and 「ありがたい」 comes from 「有り難い」 (rare, hard to come by), which developed into “worthy of thanks”. Literally the sentence says “if I could receive your doing ..., that would be something precious to me”. It only states a hypothesis and your own feeling; it neither commands nor asks directly, and leaves the decision to the other person, which is why it works as a soft request. Replace 「いただける」 with 「もらえる」 and the respect level drops; replace 「ありがたい」 with 「幸い」 or 「助かる」 and the degree of formality shifts accordingly.

meaning: A formal hearsay expression used in letters: “I have heard that ...”.
connection: Noun + の／verb・adjective plain form + 由

senses.label: I hear that
senses.meaning: Shows news you heard from someone else. Used mainly in letters, cards and formal speeches. It is formal and old-fashioned, and almost never used in conversation.
senses.connection: Noun + の由／verb・adjective plain form + 由 (followed by 「、」, 「を伺い」, 「承りました」, etc.)
examples: I am delighted to hear that you are in good health.
I was very surprised to hear that your father was hospitalized.
I hear you will be coming to Tokyo soon. I look forward to seeing you.

senses.label: Relaying a message
senses.meaning: 「〜との由」 relays what the other person told you, like 「〜とのこと」. Often used in replies to confirm you got their message.
senses.connection: Plain form + との由
examples: I understand that you will be absent tomorrow.
I was relieved to hear that you got home safely.

notes: Here 「由」 is read 「よし」, not 「ゆう」 or 「ゆ」.
It is for news you have heard about the other person or a third party, not for your own affairs: ✕ 「私は来月結婚する由です」 → ○ 「私事ですが、来月結婚することになりました」.
Use it only in formal writing such as letters, greeting cards, and speeches. In chat or ordinary emails it sounds stiff and affected; there you would say 「〜と伺いました」 or 「〜とのことで」.
When you mention the other person or their family, match it with honorific wording, as in 「ご健勝の由」 or 「ご入院の由」. Writing just 「入院した由」 about an elder sounds cold and impolite.
The 「由」 in 「知る由もない」 means “means, way”, so it means “there is no way to know”. It has nothing to do with hearsay, so do not confuse them.

daily.title: Writing a New Year's card
daily.description: You write a New Year's card to a former teacher you have not seen for a long time.
daily.example: I am very glad to hear that you are doing well as always.

daily.title: Reading old letters
daily.description: You come across it in a novel or a collection of letters.
daily.example: I have heard that Mother is ill, and I am worried.

work.title: Formal business reply
work.description: You reply formally after hearing from a client.
work.example: We have learned of your company's relocation and offer our sincere congratulations.

work.title: Confirming a schedule
work.description: You reply to confirm a change the other side told you about.
work.example: We have noted that the dates of your business trip have changed.

etymology: 「由」 (よし) originally meant “reason, origin”, then “the content or gist of something”. Classical texts often used 「〜の由申す」 (to report the content of something). It later became fixed in letters as “I have heard that ...”.

similar.title: 〜とのことだ
similar.explanation: 「〜とのことだ」 is used in speech and general writing, and often in business emails. 「〜由」 is more archaic and appears only in formal writing such as letters and speeches; 「との由」 can be seen as the letter-style version of 「とのこと」.

similar.title: 〜そうだ（hearsay）
similar.explanation: 「〜そうだ」 is the most ordinary hearsay form and works in everyday conversation. 「〜由」 has the formality of letter style and is mostly used about the other person or their family.

similar.title: 〜ということだ（hearsay・conclusion）
similar.explanation: 「〜ということだ」 can express hearsay and also a conclusion (“in other words ...”). 「〜由」 only reports news you have heard and never expresses a conclusion.

formation: 「由」 (よし) is originally a noun meaning “reason, the content of a matter”, and here it works as a formal noun that is modified by what comes before it: noun + 「の」, or a verb/adjective in plain form. Literally 「〜の由」 is “the matter that ...”; in a letter you write “... (this is the matter) I have learned”, and so the noun itself comes to carry the sense of “news that I have heard”. The 「と」 in 「との由」 is the quotation particle, making clear that what follows was conveyed by someone else, like 「とのこと」. Because the core is a noun, it is often followed by 「、」 and then a comment, or by 「承りました」 or 「伺いました」 to say you have received the news.

meaning: “If it were ..., that would be different, but ...”. It first gives an exception, then states the usual conclusion.
connection: Noun / plain form + なら別だが

senses.label: Exception
senses.meaning: First name a special case as an exception. The second half gives your judgment for normal cases, usually a negative one.
senses.connection: Noun / verb・adjective plain form (のなら) + なら別だが、〜
examples: If it's urgent, that's different, but could you leave it until tomorrow?
A professional would be another matter, but it's dangerous for an amateur to climb this mountain alone.
If he wants to, that's another story, but there's no need to force him to join.

senses.label: That changes things
senses.meaning: 「それなら話は別だ」 is used on its own. It means that if the condition changes, your attitude changes too. Common in speech.
senses.connection: それなら／〜なら + 話は別だ
examples: If the company pays the costs, that's a different story.
What, he's coming too? Well, that changes things.

notes: With a noun, attach 「なら」 directly without 「だ」: ✕ 「プロだなら別だが」 → ○ 「プロなら別だが」. With verbs and adjectives you can say 「〜（の）なら別だが」.
The speaker's real point is in the second clause; the first clause only rules out one exception. Do not put the conclusion you actually want to express in the first part.
「それなら話は別だ」 means “if that is the case, my attitude changes” (usually from refusing to agreeing), not “that is a separate topic and has nothing to do with this”.
It is different from 「〜とは別に」 (apart from ...): 「仕事とは別に趣味がある」 means “apart from work, I also have a hobby”, with no sense of hypothesis or exception.

daily.title: Turning down a friend
daily.description: A friend invites you out on the weekend, but you are busy.
daily.example: If it rains, that's different, but I've got work in the field this weekend.

daily.title: Stopping a family member's purchase
daily.description: Someone in your family wants expensive fitness equipment.
daily.example: If you'd use it every day, fine, but you'll get bored of it quickly, won't you?

work.title: Explaining the rules
work.description: You explain the return policy to a customer.
work.example: Initial defects are an exception, but we cannot accept returns once the package is opened.

work.title: Discussing the budget
work.description: You give your view on extra investment in a meeting.
work.example: If we could be sure of the results, it would be a different story, but at this point I can't support it.

etymology: Made of 「なら」 (if), the noun 「別」 (different, separate) and the contrastive 「だが」 (but). Literally “if it were ..., things would be different, but ...”. It became a fixed way to state an exception and then a conclusion.

similar.title: 〜ならともかく
similar.explanation: 「〜ならともかく」 also means “if it were ..., fine, but ...” and is almost the same, so the two can be swapped. 「ともかく」 leans toward “setting aside for now”, 「別だ」 toward “that is an exception”, and the latter is more common in speech.

similar.title: 〜ならいざしらず／〜はいざしらず
similar.explanation: 「〜ならいざしらず」 has the same meaning but is more literary and slightly old-fashioned, often found in written text. 「〜なら別だが」 works in both speech and writing.

similar.title: 〜は別として
similar.explanation: Both contain 「別」. 「〜は別として」 excludes something from the discussion and is not hypothetical; 「〜なら別だが」 is a hypothetical condition meaning “if that were the case”.

formation: It is made of the conditional 「なら」, the noun 「別」 (another, different), the copula 「だ」, and the contrastive 「が」. Literally 「Aなら別だ」 means “if it is A, that is a different matter”, that is, A is set apart as an exception. Then 「が」 turns the sentence around: “but in fact it is not A”, which leads into a judgment about the general case. Because the first part is set up as an “exception”, the second part is naturally a conclusion about the usual case, and it is mostly a negative or pessimistic one. If you drop 「が」 and end with 「話は別だ」, only the idea “if the condition changes, the conclusion changes” remains, which is often used to state an attitude in conversation.

meaning: “I did ..., which was fine, but then ...”. The action itself was okay, but the result was not.
connection: Verb ta-form + はいいが／のはいいが

senses.label: Good start, bad result
senses.meaning: The first part is something already done that seems fine. The second part shows the trouble that followed. It often sounds regretful, self-mocking or critical.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form + はいいが (のはいいが／はいいけど)
examples: Quitting my job on impulse was all well and good, but I can't find a new one.
I left the house all right, but I hadn't decided where to go.
Getting a dog was great, but walking it is tough.

senses.label: Fine up to that point
senses.meaning: 「〜たまではよかったが」 means things went well up to a point, but then something went wrong. It stresses that only the first half was good.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form + まではよかったが
examples: Everything was fine until we reached the summit, but we got lost on the way down.
Passing the exam was great, but I can't pay the admission fee.

notes: The second clause must be a negative result such as trouble or a predicament: ✕ 「留学したはいいが、毎日楽しい」 → ○ 「留学したはいいが、言葉が通じず苦労している」.
The first part must be in the ta-form, for something already done. 「行くのはいいけど、気をつけてね」 (going is fine, but be careful) is “agreement + a warning”, not this pattern.

Used about someone else's actions, it carries criticism or sarcasm: saying 「部長が企画を通したはいいが……」 about your boss is like pointing out his faults to his face, and is very rude. It is mostly used about yourself (self-mockery) or a third party.

daily.title: Regretting an online purchase
daily.description: You complain to a friend about an impulse buy.
daily.example: I bought it on sale, but it was the wrong size.

daily.title: Trouble on a trip
daily.description: You talk about an awkward moment while traveling.
daily.example: I made it to the airport, but then I realized I'd forgotten my passport.

daily.title: Reading an opinion piece
daily.description: An article criticizes a policy.
daily.example: They created the system, but hardly anyone uses it.

work.title: Project review
work.description: You reflect on problems with a project in a meeting.
work.example: We introduced the new system, but few employees can use it well.

work.title: Reporting to your boss
work.description: You explain a problem that came up while carrying out a plan.
work.example: Winning the contract went well, but it looks like we won't make the deadline.

etymology: Made of the verb ta-form, the topic marker 「は」, 「いい」 (good, fine) and the contrastive 「が」. Literally “doing ... was fine, but ...”. The positive first half highlights the problem in the second half.

similar.title: 〜ものの
similar.explanation: 「〜たものの」 also means “I did it, but ...” and can replace it, but it is more literary and more objective. 「〜たはいいが」 is more colloquial, and the feelings of self-mockery and regret are stronger.

similar.title: 〜ことは〜が
similar.explanation: 「行ったことは行ったが」 means “I did go, but (not enough, not as hoped)”, focusing on the action being incomplete. 「〜たはいいが」 focuses on new trouble arising after the action.

similar.title: 〜こそ〜が（although ... but）
similar.explanation: 「謝りこそしたが」 means “I did apologize, but ...”; it is written-style and sounds firmer. 「〜たはいいが」 is more colloquial, and what follows is mostly a predicament you yourself are in.

formation: It is made of the ta-form of a verb, the topic particle 「は」, 「いい」, and the contrastive 「が」. The ta-form shows the action is done; 「は」 picks out “having done this” as the thing to evaluate, with a contrast: “this part itself is fine”. That contrast implies “this is the only good part”, so after 「が」 the sentence naturally turns to the problem that followed. Affirming first and then turning around makes the drop larger, which produces a tone of regret, self-mockery, or criticism. 「〜たまではよかったが」 uses 「まで」 to draw the line “the good part ends here”, which says this more explicitly.

meaning: After doing something, things stay that way, and what should have happened next never happens.
connection: Verb ta-form + なり (〜ない／〜たなりで)

senses.label: Ever since then
senses.meaning: After an action happens, nothing changes afterward. The second part is usually negative, often with surprise or worry. Written and literary.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form + なり、〜ない
examples: My son went out this morning and still hasn't come back.
He sat down in the chair and never said a word.
He borrowed the book and never gave it back.

senses.label: As it was
senses.meaning: 「〜たなりで」 means doing the next thing while keeping the state of the first action, like 「〜たままで」.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form + なりで
examples: I was so tired I fell asleep with my clothes on.
He came into the room with his shoes still on.

notes: A change of form changes the whole meaning: 「座るなり話し始めた」 (started talking the moment he sat down) ↔ 「座ったなり話さなかった」 (sat down and then never said anything). Dictionary form + なり means “as soon as”, ta-form + なり means “it stayed that way afterward”.
The second clause is generally “something that should have happened did not” (negative) and cannot be a new action: ✕ 「家に帰ったなり、すぐ寝た」 → ○ 「家に帰るなり、すぐ寝た」.
In everyday conversation 「〜たなり」 sounds very literary and dated; in speech use 「〜たきり」 or 「〜たまま」.
It is a different grammar point from 「〜なりに」 (in one's own way, as in 「私なりに」); do not mix them up.

daily.title: Worried about family
daily.description: A family member went out and hasn't come back. You tell a neighbor.
daily.example: My father went out for a walk and hasn't been back for three hours.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A novel describes a character's silence.
daily.example: She hung her head and said nothing.

work.title: Complaining about a partner company
work.description: The other company received the materials and then went silent.
work.example: They received the materials and we haven't heard a thing since.

etymology: 「なり」 comes from the classical copula 「なり」 and the noun 「なり」 (shape, appearance). 「〜たなり」 means “in the state of having done ...”, close to 「〜たまま」 and 「〜たきり」.

similar.title: 〜きり・〜たきり
similar.explanation: 「〜たきり」 is the closest in meaning, also “after ..., never ... again”, and is the most common form in modern Japanese. 「〜たなり」 means the same but is more literary and slightly old-fashioned.

similar.title: 〜まま
similar.explanation: 「〜たまま」 only says that a state continues and can be used for neutral facts (窓を開けたまま寝た). 「〜たなりで」 is equivalent, but 「〜たなり、〜ない」 also carries a sense of surprise or worry that nothing followed.

similar.title: 〜なり（as soon as）
similar.explanation: Both are built with 「なり」. 「〜るなり」 takes the dictionary form and means “as soon as ...”; 「〜たなり」 takes the ta-form and means the state continues and nothing follows. The meanings are almost opposite.

formation: It is made of the ta-form of a verb plus 「なり」. This 「なり」 is generally thought to have the same origin as the 「なり」 in 「身なり」 (one's appearance) and 「弓なり」 (arched like a bow), meaning “shape, appearance”. 「〜たなり」 is “the way things looked when ... was done”, showing that the state after the action stays as it is and does not change. If the state does not change, the next expected action did not happen, so the second clause is mostly negative (went out and never came back, sat down and said nothing). Adding the particle 「で」 of manner gives 「〜たなりで」, “doing the next thing in that state”, equivalent to 「〜たままで」.

meaning: Repeating the same verb means “I want to, but I can't”. Something stops you from doing it.
connection: Verb dictionary form + に + same verb in negative potential form

senses.label: Want to but can't
senses.meaning: The speaker really wants to do something but can't, because of the situation, their position or their feelings. It conveys frustration or helplessness.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + に + same verb potential + ない (ず)
examples: My boss is still here, so I can't leave even though I want to.
He seems to have reasons he just can't talk about.
Now that I've started, I can't stop even if I want to.

senses.label: Can't laugh, can't cry
senses.meaning: 「泣くに泣けない」 and 「笑うに笑えない」 are set phrases. They describe something so awkward or absurd you don't know whether to laugh or cry.
senses.connection: 泣くに泣けない／笑うに笑えない (+ 話・失敗)
examples: Failing by just one point is too sad even to cry about.
I made a mistake that was no laughing matter.

notes: Use the dictionary form first and the negative potential of the same verb after it: ✕ 「帰りに帰れない」 ✕ 「帰るに帰らない」 → ○ 「帰るに帰れない」.
It means “I want to do it and could in principle, but circumstances prevent me”, and cannot be used for plain lack of ability: ✕ 「泳ぐに泳げない」 (you simply cannot swim) → ○ 「泳げない」.
「言うに言えない」 (hard to bring oneself to say) and 「言うに言われぬ」 (impossible to put into words) are different: 「言うに言われぬ美しさ」 is “beauty beyond words”, not “too embarrassed to say”.

daily.title: Can't leave the party first
daily.description: The party is in full swing. You want to leave but feel awkward.
daily.example: Everyone was having so much fun that I couldn't bring myself to leave.

daily.title: Confiding in a friend
daily.description: You tell a friend there is something you can't talk about.
daily.example: It's a family matter, so I just can't tell people about it.

daily.title: Telling a funny mishap
daily.description: You tell a story that is both funny and sad.
daily.example: The rain stopped right after I bought an umbrella. I couldn't even laugh.

work.title: No backing out of a project
work.description: A lot of money has gone into the project, and you can't pull out.
work.example: Now that we've invested this much, there's no backing down.

work.title: Work you can't refuse
work.description: You complain to a coworker about work you couldn't turn down.
work.example: The department head asked me personally, so I just couldn't say no.

etymology: Here 「に」 shows purpose: 「帰るに」 means “wanting to go home”. Literally “I want to go home, but I can't”. Repeating the verb stresses the gap between the wish and reality.

similar.title: 〜(よ)うにも〜ない
similar.explanation: It is the closest in meaning, but the volitional form comes first: 「帰ろうにも帰れない」. It stresses “even if I try, I cannot”, mostly because of objective conditions; 「帰るに帰れない」 is mostly because of obligations, position, or other mental hesitation.

similar.title: 〜ようがない
similar.explanation: 「〜ようがない」 means there is simply no way, no means to begin (連絡しようがない). 「〜に〜ない」 means there is a way, but you cannot do it because of hesitation.

similar.title: 〜わけにはいかない
similar.explanation: 「〜わけにはいかない」 says calmly that “you cannot do this” on grounds of reason or common sense. 「〜に〜ない」 emphasizes the helpless feeling of wanting to do it but being unable to.

formation: It is made of a verb in dictionary form + 「に」 + the negative of the potential form of the same verb. This 「に」 shows purpose or intention, close to the 「に」 in 「買いに行く」, so 「帰るに」 means “wanting to go home”. The second half uses the negative potential, which talks about “can or cannot” rather than “want or not want”. Putting the same verb before and after sets a wish against reality, and the gap between them creates the helplessness of “I want to ..., but I can't”. Because the stress is on being blocked by circumstances, social obligations, or one's position, rather than on unwillingness, it is often used in situations with something unsayable or where you cannot back out.

meaning: Repeating one verb or listing several verbs shows things happening one after another in surprising numbers. Often with surprise or exasperation.
connection: Verb dictionary form・ta-form + わ + verb dictionary form・ta-form + わ

senses.label: One after another
senses.meaning: Repeating the same verb, as in 「出るわ出るわ」, means the same thing happens again and again in surprising numbers. It sounds surprised or exclamatory.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + わ + same verb dictionary form + わ
examples: When I checked the books, the mistakes just kept coming. There was no end to them.
It rained and rained and didn't stop for three days.

senses.label: One bad thing after another
senses.meaning: Listing different verbs means several (usually bad) things happened at once or in a row. Often 「〜わで」 is followed by 「大変だ」 or 「さんざんだ」.
senses.connection: Verb A + わ + verb B + わ (で)
examples: What with the rain and the wind, it was a terrible day.
He ate and drank so much that he spent ten thousand yen all by himself.
I lost my wallet and missed the train. It was a total disaster.

notes: It attaches only to inflected words such as verbs and adjectives, not directly to nouns: ✕ 「雨わ風わで大変だった」 → ○ 「雨は降るわ風は吹くわで大変だった」.
It is mostly used for complaining and telling of bad luck. Using it about the behavior of a superior or client (「部長は飲むわ騒ぐわで……」) is like criticizing him in public, and is very rude.
It is strongly colloquial and is not used in formal documents such as reports and emails; in formal situations use 「〜たり〜たりして」 or 「〜うえに」.
This 「わ」 is not the feminine sentence-final particle; men and women can both use it. Do not confuse it with the standalone sentence-ending 「行くわ」 (a feminine tone).

daily.title: Talking about a big cleanup
daily.description: You tell a friend what happened when you tidied your room.
daily.example: When I cleaned out the closet, old photos just kept turning up.

daily.title: Complaining about a trip
daily.description: You complain to your family after a trip.
daily.example: The roads were jammed and the inn was dirty. What a miserable trip.

work.title: A chaotic day at work
work.description: You tell a coworker about a hectic day.
work.example: What with the phone ringing and customers coming in, I didn't even get to eat lunch.

etymology: 「わ」 comes from the exclamatory sentence-ending particle 「わ」. Repeating or listing exclamatory phrases created a “...! ...!” list that shows things happening nonstop and surprisingly.

similar.title: 〜わ〜わで
similar.explanation: It is the same construction followed by 「で」, used specifically to lead into an evaluation that “the result was bad”; 「〜わ〜わ」 can also stand alone to marvel at quantity (出るわ出るわ).

similar.title: 〜やら〜やら
similar.explanation: 「〜やら〜やら」 also lists things that happen one after another, and it can take nouns (宿題やら掃除やら) with a more neutral tone. 「〜わ〜わ」 takes only inflected words and carries stronger surprise and complaint.

similar.title: 〜し
similar.explanation: 「〜し〜し」 calmly lists several reasons. 「〜わ〜わ」 has a strong exclamatory tone and stresses that things keep coming one after another until you cannot cope.

formation: It is made of the terminal form of an inflected word + the sentence-final particle 「わ」, repeated or placed side by side. 「わ」 was originally a sentence-final particle of exclamation and emphasis, like “... oh my”. Saying clauses with 「わ」 one after another is like the speaker counting things off while exclaiming. Repeating the same verb (出るわ出るわ) means the same thing keeps coming; listing different verbs (降るわ吹くわ) means several things (mostly bad) hit at once. Adding 「で」 for cause lets you connect an evaluation of the result such as 「大変だ」 or 「さんざんだ」.

meaning: “Worthy of ...”, “living up to ...”. Actions or results match a reputation, status or expectations.
connection: Noun + に恥じない／に恥じぬ

senses.label: Worthy of the name
senses.meaning: Often follows 「名」, 「称号」 or 「肩書き」. It means the actual performance lives up to the name or status. Used in evaluations or statements of resolve.
senses.connection: Noun (の名／称号) + に恥じない (に恥じぬ) + noun
examples: I want to play a match worthy of the champion's title.
He fought in a way worthy of a title favorite.

senses.label: Living up to expectations
senses.meaning: Follows 「期待」, 「信頼」, 「伝統」, etc. It means not letting them down. 「〜に恥じないよう (に)」 is often used to express determination.
senses.connection: Noun (期待／信頼／伝統) + に恥じないよう (に)
examples: We will do our best to live up to your expectations.
They have kept a flavor worthy of a hundred-year tradition.

notes: Use the negative of the verb 「恥じる」, not an adjective: ✕ 「チャンピオンの名に恥ずかしくない試合」 → ○ 「チャンピオンの名に恥じない試合」.
The particle is 「に」: ✕ 「期待を恥じない」 → ○ 「期待に恥じない」.
The first part must be something positive and worthy of respect, such as honor, expectations, or tradition. With a negative noun it turns sarcastic: 「悪名に恥じない」 means “living up to its bad reputation”.

Judging whether a superior or elder is “worthy of his position” is itself condescending, so saying 「部長の名に恥じない」 to your boss's face is rude. It is mostly used to state your own resolve or to evaluate groups and works.

daily.title: Watching sports news
daily.description: Sports news praises a player's performance.
daily.example: It was a performance worthy of the national team.

daily.title: Graduation speech
daily.description: A graduate gives a speech at the ceremony.
daily.example: I will become someone worthy of being called a graduate of this school.

work.title: Inaugural speech
work.description: A new company president speaks at their inauguration.
work.example: I will aim for management worthy of the founder's philosophy.

work.title: Company advertising
work.description: Promotional copy for a long-established business.
work.example: We deliver quality worthy of our long-established name.

etymology: 「恥じる」 means “to feel ashamed”, and 「に」 marks what you compare yourself against. Literally “not ashamed in the face of ...”, which came to mean “worthy of ...”.

similar.title: 〜に足る
similar.explanation: 「〜に足る」 means “worth ..., enough to ...” (信頼に足る人物) and focuses on whether something qualifies. 「〜に恥じない」 focuses on living up to a reputation or expectation without disgracing it, with the nuance of “not shameful”.

similar.title: 〜に値する
similar.explanation: 「〜に値する」 means “deserving (praise, a read, etc.)” and is mostly preceded by action nouns (称賛に値する). 「〜に恥じない」 is preceded by titles and expectations, meaning your performance is worthy of them.

similar.title: 〜たる
similar.explanation: 「教師たる者」 stresses how a person of a certain status “should be”, a normative demand. 「教師の名に恥じない」 is an evaluation or a resolve: conduct worthy of that status.

formation: It is made of 「に」 marking the object of comparison, the verb 「恥じる」 (to feel ashamed), and the negative 「ない」. 「Aに恥じる」 means “to be ashamed before A”, that is, you do not measure up to A; negated, it means “not ashamed before A”. From “not ashamed” it extends to “worthy of A, not unworthy of A”. Because the core is “not disgracing”, the first part must be something worth respecting, such as honor, expectations, or tradition. 「恥じぬ」 uses the classical negative 「ぬ」 and sounds more solemn, often seen in speeches and headlines.

meaning: Attaches quoted content directly to a noun: “a (message, opinion, etc.) saying that ...”.
connection: Plain form / 〜ようにと + との + noun (連絡・知らせ・意見, etc.)

senses.label: A message saying that
senses.meaning: 「との」 comes before nouns for messages and notices and gives their content. Like 「〜という」, but more written and concise.
senses.connection: Plain form + との + 連絡／知らせ／報告／返事
examples: We received word that he will be off tomorrow.
I got a notice saying the meeting has been postponed.

senses.label: Opinions and views
senses.meaning: Followed by 「意見」, 「声」, 「見方」, 「指摘」, etc., it gives the content of an opinion or view. Very common in the news.
senses.connection: Plain form + との + 意見／声／見方／指摘
examples: Many people also say the price increase is unavoidable.
The prevailing view is that the economy is recovering.

senses.label: Orders and requests
senses.meaning: 「〜ようにとの」 followed by 「指示」, 「命令」, 「電話」, etc. gives the content of an order or request.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form・nai-form + ようにとの + 指示／命令／電話
examples: I got a call telling me to come right away.
An instruction was issued not to go outside.

notes: When a noun comes before 「との」, it often means “with ...”, which is completely different: 「部長との話」 is “a talk with the manager”, while 「部長が来るとの話」 is “word that the manager is coming”.
Only nouns of speech or thought content (連絡, 意見, 指示, etc.) can follow, not ordinary nouns: ✕ 「明日休むとの人」 → ○ 「明日休むという人」.
It is strongly written-style and rarely spoken; in conversation use 「〜って連絡があった」 or 「〜という話」.

daily.title: A school notice
daily.description: Parents hear that school is closed.
daily.example: The school contacted us to say classes are canceled because of heavy snow.

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: The news reports public opinion.
daily.example: Calls for a review of the system keep coming in.

work.title: Business email
work.description: You pass on a client's reply.
work.example: We received a reply from the client saying there are no problems with the contract terms.

work.title: Internal instructions
work.description: You pass on an instruction from a superior.
work.example: The department head has instructed everyone to attend.

etymology: Made of the quotation particle 「と」 plus the linking 「の」. 「と」 can't modify a noun on its own, but adding 「の」 links the quote to a noun. It works like 「という」.

similar.title: 〜という（called）
similar.explanation: 「〜という + noun」 can modify any noun and works in both speech and writing. 「〜との」 is more concise and literary, and can only take nouns of content such as news and opinions.

similar.title: 〜とのことだ
similar.explanation: Both are built from 「と + の」. 「〜とのことだ」 goes at the end of a sentence to report hearsay (“I hear that ...”); 「〜との + noun」 modifies a noun inside a sentence and explains the content of the news or opinion.

similar.title: 〜由
similar.explanation: 「〜との由」 is also 「との」 followed by a noun, meaning “the matter that (the other person) has informed me of ...”, but it is used only in formal writing such as letters.

formation: It is made of the quotative case particle 「と」 plus the attributive particle 「の」. 「と」 marks the content of speaking or thinking, but it can only attach to verbs such as 「言う」, 「思う」, and 「連絡する」, and cannot modify a noun directly. Adding 「の」 lets the quoted content connect straight to a noun, working like 「という」 with 「いう」 left out. Because it comes from the quotation of “saying and thinking”, the noun that follows must also be one that can “hold content”, such as 「連絡」, 「意見」, and 「指示」. 「ようにとの」 quotes a whole command 「〜ように」 and then attaches a noun.

meaning: Means “before ...” in time, or points out a problem at an even more basic level: “that's not even the issue yet”.
connection: Noun / verb dictionary form + 以前 (の問題／に)

senses.label: Before
senses.meaning: Refers to the period before a point in time or an event. More formal than 「〜前」 and mostly used in writing.
senses.connection: Noun (era・time) / verb dictionary form + 以前
examples: In Japan before the Meiji era, eating meat was not common.
This problem existed even before he joined the company.

senses.label: Not even at that stage
senses.meaning: 「〜以前の問題」 and 「〜以前に」 mean even something more basic hasn't been done, so the first thing isn't even the issue. It sounds critical.
senses.connection: Noun + 以前の問題だ／以前の話だ／以前に
examples: This isn't even a question of ability.
That's not even a matter of common sense. It's more basic than that.
Never mind honorifics; you can't even greet people properly.

notes: In rules and contracts 「〇日以前」 includes that day, unlike 「〇日より前」 (not including it); misreading a deadline can cause real loss.
「〜以前の問題だ」 is a heavy criticism, meaning “you have not even done the most basic thing”. Telling a superior or client 「それは常識以前の問題です」 is very rude.
After a verb, use the dictionary form: ✕ 「入社した以前」 → ○ 「入社する以前」／「入社以前」.

daily.title: Scolding a child
daily.description: A parent criticizes a child's lifestyle.
daily.example: Never mind your grades; first, get up properly in the morning.

daily.title: Watching a history program
daily.description: A TV program covers ancient history.
daily.example: Not much is known about history before writing arrived.

work.title: Pointing out a subordinate's problem
work.description: A manager points out a basic problem with a report.
work.example: Before we even get to the content, please meet your deadlines.

work.title: Academic paper
work.description: A paper sets the time range of the research.
work.example: This study mainly analyzes materials from before the war.

etymology: 「以前」 is a Sino-Japanese word: 「以」 marks a boundary and 「前」 means “before”. It first meant “before a certain time”. From “earlier in time or order” it extended to “more basic in level”, giving the “not even at that stage” use.

similar.title: 〜まえに
similar.explanation: Both contain 「前」. 「〜前に」 is the ordinary “before ...” and common in speech. 「〜以前」 is more formal, mostly written, and only it can mean “it is not even a question of ...”.

similar.title: 〜どころか
similar.explanation: 「敬語どころか挨拶もできない」 and 「敬語以前に挨拶ができていない」 are close in meaning: both say “never mind ..., you can't even do the more basic thing”. 「どころか」 focuses on the more extreme thing named in the second clause, 「以前」 on the problem lying at a more basic level.

similar.title: 〜に先立って
similar.explanation: 「〜に先立って」 means preparing in advance before something (開会に先立って). 「〜以前」 only gives a time range before a point and carries no sense of advance preparation.

formation: 「以前」 is a Sino-Japanese word: 「以」 marks a point as the boundary, and 「前」 means before, so together it is “the side before that boundary”. After a time or an event it simply means “before ...”. From “earlier in time or order” it extends to “earlier in level, more basic”: 「能力以前の問題」 means “the problem lies at a stage before ability”. That is, the premise has not even been reached, so the first item is out of the question, which gives a critical, reproachful tone. 「〜以前に」 means “never mind ..., the more basic thing is ...”.

meaning: An objective guess used in news and other writing: “is believed to ...”, “is thought to be ...”.
connection: Noun / plain form + とみられる (とみられている)

senses.label: Is believed to
senses.meaning: A guess based on the available facts. It sounds objective and careful and avoids stating things as certain. Especially common in news reports.
senses.connection: Noun / verb・adjective plain form + とみられる／とみられている
examples: The accident is believed to have been caused by the driver falling asleep.
The culprit is thought to be a man in his thirties.
This summer is expected to be hotter than usual.

senses.label: Modifying a noun
senses.meaning: 「〜とみられる + noun」 means “a ... believed to be ...”. In the news it refers to people or things not yet identified.
senses.connection: Noun + とみられる + noun
examples: A man believed to be the culprit was arrested.
They are investigating the house thought to be where the fire started.

notes: Here 「みられる」 is passive (is regarded as), not potential (can see): 「富士山が見られる」 means “you can see Mt. Fuji”, while 「犯人とみられる」 means “is believed to be the culprit”.
The one speculating is an outside party such as the police, experts, or the media, so it is not used to state your own opinion: ✕ (in a meeting) 「私は原因が設計ミスとみられます」 → ○ 「原因は設計ミスだと考えます」.
In everyday conversation it sounds like a news broadcast and is stiff; in speech say 「〜らしい」 or 「〜みたいだ」.

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: The TV news reports the cause of a fire.
daily.example: The fire is believed to have been caused by a carelessly discarded cigarette.

daily.title: Reading the weather forecast
daily.description: A weather forecast in the newspaper.
daily.example: The typhoon is expected to make landfall over the weekend.

work.title: Business news
work.description: A report on a company's earnings forecast.
work.example: The company's profits are expected to reach a record high.

work.title: Market analysis report
work.description: An analysis report states its conclusion.
work.example: Demand is expected to keep falling.

etymology: Here 「みる」 doesn't mean “to see” but “to judge, to consider”, and 「みられる」 is its passive. Literally “is judged to be ...”. Because the one judging is not named, it became an objective news expression.

similar.title: 〜とされる
similar.explanation: 「〜とされる」 expresses what is generally accepted or an established view (〜が原因とされる). 「〜とみられる」 is speculation based on current signs and is not yet settled.

similar.title: 〜ものと思われる
similar.explanation: 「〜ものと思われる」 is mostly the speaker's own careful judgment, common in reports and papers. 「〜とみられる」 mostly refers to a judgment made by outside parties such as the police or experts.

similar.title: 〜と考えられる
similar.explanation: 「〜と考えられる」 stresses a conclusion reached by logical reasoning and can be used for your own argument. 「〜とみられる」 stresses speculation from circumstances and signs, with a strong news flavor.

formation: It is made of the quotative 「と」, the verb 「みる」, and the passive auxiliary 「られる」. Here 「みる」 does not mean “to look with the eyes” but “to judge, to regard” (as in 「甘くみる」 and 「様子をみる」). 「Aとみる」 means “to judge it to be A”, and the passive 「Aとみられる」 means “is judged to be A”. A passive sentence does not name the one who judges, so it sounds as if “society and the parties concerned think so”, producing the objective, cautious tone of news speculation. Adding 「ている」 gives 「とみられている」, meaning this view already exists and is widely accepted.
